title: Anonymized Dataset on Physical Literacy and Football Shooting Skill Acquisition in Children: A Comparison of Linear and Nonlinear Pedagogies
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This dataset contains anonymized participant-level data from a randomized study examining the effects of a physical literacy-based preparation program and subsequent linear and nonlinear pedagogical approaches on football shooting skill acquisition in children aged 8–9 years. The study involved 52 male children assigned to four experimental conditions based on physical literacy intervention (physical literacy-based program or regular physical education) and pedagogical approach (linear or nonlinear). The dataset includes demographic and anthropometric characteristics (age, height, weight, and body mass index), as well as pre- and post-intervention scores for physical literacy (PLAYfun total score) and football shooting performance. These data can be used to examine changes in physical literacy and shooting performance and to investigate the effects of physical literacy-based preparation and pedagogical approaches on motor skill acquisition. Participant identifiers are anonymized. The dataset is provided in Excel format for research transparency and potential secondary analysis.

title: Effects of Game-Based Nonlinear Pedagogy on Metabolic Biomarkers, Inflammatory Cytokines, and Physical Fitness in Children with Down Syndrome: Moderation Analysis of Baseline Cardiorespiratory Fitness
abstract: This is a preregistration for a randomized controlled trial (RCT) that investigated the effects of a 16-week game-based nonlinear pedagogy (NP) intervention (BOOST-DS) on metabolic biomarkers (HOMA-IR, fasting glucose, fasting insulin), inflammatory cytokines (TNF-α, IL-6, CRP), and physical fitness (body composition, cardiorespiratory fitness, muscular strength, flexibility) in children with Down syndrome (DS) aged 8–12 years. The study also examined whether baseline cardiorespiratory fitness (VO₂peak) moderated the intervention effects.

title: Beyond the Ring: A Comparative Scientific Analysis of Mixed Martial Arts (MMA) and Real Martial Art (RMA) – Training Objectives, Combat Adaptability, Situational Awareness, and Real-World Self-Defense
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This research presents a comparative analytical study of Mixed Martial Arts (MMA) and Real Martial Art (RMA), examining their training philosophies, technical foundations, tactical objectives, and applications in competitive combat and real-world self-defense. The study explores the distinction between regulated competitive fighting and broader defensive preparedness, with particular attention to situational awareness, threat recognition, decision-making, environmental adaptability, physical conditioning, and defensive movement. MMA is examined as an established competitive combat sport integrating striking, wrestling, grappling, and submission techniques within a regulated sporting environment. Real Martial Art (RMA), founded by Tarek Sayed Ibrahim, is examined as a developing reality-based martial arts system designed to integrate combat skills with defensive awareness, practical decision-making, avoidance, and survival-oriented principles. The research draws upon published scientific literature concerning combat sports, injury epidemiology, motor learning, ecological dynamics, and decision-making under pressure. A multidimensional framework is proposed for future empirical research, including technical proficiency, physical performance, situational awareness, defensive decision-making, and escape performance. The study does not claim absolute superiority of either system. Instead, it identifies their different objectives and examines how competitive combat skills and reality-based defensive training may provide complementary capabilities. title: Strokes towards more evidence-based swimming lessons: motor learning and motivation in children
abstract: Swimming skills are essential for safety, recreation, and health. However, basic swimming skills are not always retained or transferred to real-world aquatic settings after initial acquisition. In addition, individuals may lack the motivation to continue swimming and maintain their skills. Identifying effective motor learning methods that promote skill acquisition, retention, transfer, and sustained motivation is therefore important for strengthening evidence-based swimming lessons. The aim of this thesis was to help make swimming lessons more evidence-based by examining how children can learn swimming skills effectively and remain motivated to swim. It focused on several theoretically grounded motor learning methods: explicit verbal instruction, video modeling, analogy learning, external-focus-of-attention learning, and the constraints-led approach (CLA). It also considered motivation from the perspective of self-determination theory (SDT), which emphasizes autonomy, competence, and relatedness as key drivers for intrinsic motivation. Chapter 2 examined current practices in Dutch swimming lessons designed to motivate children. To this end, 128 lessons taught by various instructors were observed. Instructors generally supported children’s need for relatedness, but often thwarted autonomy and offered limited competence support. Lessons based on SDT principles scored higher on all three needs, with a significant difference for autonomy. The teaching program was the only significant predictor of instructors’ use of SDT principles. These findings suggest that integrating SDT principles into teaching programs may improve the support of children’s psychological needs, particularly autonomy. title: TOMADA DE DECISÃO E APRENDIZAGEM TÁTICA NO FUTEBOL ESCOLAR: EVIDÊNCIAS A PARTIR DE ABORDAGENS BASEADAS EM JOGOS
abstract: O ensino de futebol na Educação Física escolar demanda experiências que integrem execução motora, leitura de jogo, cooperação e tomada de decisão. Este artigo analisa criticamente evidências sobre abordagens baseadas em jogos e seu potencial para desenvolver aprendizagem tática em turmas escolares heterogêneas. Realizou-se revisão sistematizada qualitativa com síntese narrativa de literatura científica e documentos curriculares, sem coleta de dados primários ou metanálise própria. Foram examinados os fundamentos do Teaching Games for Understanding, propostas táticas centradas no jogo, princípios da pedagogia não linear, jogos reduzidos, mediação docente e instrumentos de avaliação contextualizada. Revisões recentes indicam efeitos promissores sobre determinadas medidas de tomada de decisão, mas apontam heterogeneidade dos procedimentos, dos desfechos e da qualidade metodológica dos estudos. A análise evidencia que o jogo modificado não garante aprendizagem quando faltam objetivos claros, distribuição de oportunidades e acompanhamento das decisões. Discute-se a necessidade de articular técnica e tática, reconhecer comportamentos sem posse, assegurar participação inclusiva e diferenciar medidas de desempenho de evidências de aprendizagem duradoura. Conclui-se que abordagens baseadas em jogos oferecem recursos pedagógicos relevantes, desde que implementadas com planejamento, reflexão, avaliação criteriosa e atenção às condições da escola.

title: Perceptual-cognitive skills in talent development environments: Coaches' perspectives and practices
abstract: Despite the recognised importance of perceptual-cognitive skills (PCS) for future professional football performance, there remains limited applied research examining how practitioners engage in this area of player development. The aim of this thesis was to critically examine how PCS are identified and assessed within talent development environments in football. Recognising the critical role of PCS in talent identification (TI) and talent development (TD), this research adopted an applied perspective to evaluate current practices and identify pathways for enhancing these processes. A central objective was to bridge the gap between academic insights and practical applications, providing actionable recommendations for industry practitioners. Chapter 2 presents a scoping review of the existing literature on PCS in football, examining their support within TD contexts and identifying gaps in the research. Building on this foundation, Chapter 4 investigates academy coaches’ perceptions and approaches to identifying and assessing PCS, alongside associated challenges and the current state of educational provision in this domain. Chapter 5 extends the scope of these findings by examining the generalisability of these findings through a national survey. The findings from these chapters informed the design of Chapter 6, which explores the co-creation of a shared mental model within a football academy in the UK. This intervention aimed to improve alignment and standardisation in the identification and assessment of PCS, offering insights into its feasibility and potential impact. The findings of this thesis contribute to the evolving understanding of PCS in football, addressing practical and knowledge gaps. The work provides actionable recommendations for enhancing coaching practice

title: EXAMINATION OF THE STRATEGY OF HUNGARIAN YOUTH FOOTBALL ORGANISATIONS
abstract: Youth education is of strategic importance for sport enterprises, as it contributes to long-term sustainability and competitiveness. A well-designed youth program supports the identification and development of talent, while the strategy adopted by sports organizations influences both athlete development and the long-term operation of the organization. The research examined the entire vertical of Hungarian youth football. A well-structured strategy supports the efficient allocation of resources, the professional and infrastructural development of athletes, and the integration of home-grown players into adult teams. It can also contribute to economic stability by reducing transfer costs, supporting diversified sources of income and increasing the attractiveness of organizations to sponsors and investors. The results highlighted that talent development, and training strategies differ between academies and lower-ranked organizations. The sample also revealed limited employee involvement in setting strategic goals, which may reduce employee engagement and the effectiveness of strategy implementation in practice.

title: Physical performance indicators for talent identification in youth soccer: an umbrella review with an update of recent primary evidence
abstract: Sprint, change-of-direction (COD), jump and endurance tests are used in youth soccer selection, but differences between selected and non-selected players do not establish whether those tests predict later success. This review will synthesise systematic reviews of physical and physiological indicators associated with selection, competitive level and subsequent progression. A complementary systematic search will identify eligible primary evidence not represented in those reviews, including recent studies and earlier omissions. The two evidence streams will remain distinguishable throughout selection, appraisal and synthesis. Biological maturation, relative age and the selection context will be considered when interpreting findings.

title: Maximal Fat Oxidation Testing in Gilbert’s Syndrome: Plasma Lipid-Mobilization Signatures from Untargeted Metabolomics
abstract: Abstract Background Gilbert’s syndrome (GS), defined by an unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia, has been linked to favorable metabolic traits, including greater fat oxidation and distinct metabolite profiles. Whether GS confers a different acute plasma metabolomic response to a FatMax test remains unknown. Methods A human age- and sex-matched case–control (GS vs normobilirubinemic controls) study was conducted from March 2023 to December 2023 at the University of Vienna. After a 12-h-overnight-fast 80 participants completed a FatMax test on a cycle ergometer and from 79 the plasma metabolome was analyzed. Blood samples were collected before (baseline) and immediately after exercise. An untargeted plasma metabolomics analysis was performed via LC–MS. Results GS and controls differed significantly in serum bilirubin concentrations (GS: 33.5 ± 13.3; C: 12.2 ± 2.72; p < 0.001, in µmol/L). Apart from the expected elevations in the subclass of bilirubin in GS, the global acute metabolomic response to FatMax was broadly similar between groups. Exercise-response was similar in all participants, displaying a fat-oxidation signature post-exercise (increase in several acetylcarnitines (dodecoanylcarnitine, tetradecenoyl carnitine, (10Z,13Z,16Z,19Z)-Docosatetraenoylcarnitine), and several fatty acids (especially unsaturated fatty acids)), with a total of 231 metabolites changing in response to exercise. Individuals with higher maximal fat oxidation displayed larger immediate post-exercise increases in selected metabolites, such as fatty acids. Conclusion A submaximal FatMax exercise test elicits a robust plasma signature consistent with fatty-acid mobilization and increased fatty-acid availability for oxidation. title: The influence of differentiated instruction on students’ motivation in physical education
abstract: Background Physical education (PE) classes are intrinsically heterogeneous, yet students differing in competence, readiness, and motivation are often exposed to uniform instructional demands. Differentiated instruction has been widely advocated as a response to learner diversity, but rigorous evidence regarding its motivational consequences and underlying psychological processes remains limited. Methods We conducted a two-arm cluster-randomized longitudinal trial across 12 secondary schools in Zhengzhou, China. Forty-eight teacher–class clusters comprising 1,152 students aged 12–15 years were randomized to a 12-week differentiated-instruction intervention or usual PE. The intervention systematically adapted task challenge, instructional support, grouping, pacing, progression, and bounded choice to students’ readiness and learning needs. Assessments were completed at baseline (T0), during intervention (T1), post-intervention (T2), and follow-up (T3). The primary outcome was autonomous motivation at T2; secondary outcomes were psychological need satisfaction and frustration, controlled motivation, amotivation, and PE engagement. Three-level longitudinal mixed-effects models and multilevel longitudinal mediation models were used. Results At T2, differentiated instruction produced higher autonomous motivation than usual PE (adjusted difference = 0.49, 95% CI [0.39, 0.59]; standardized effect = 0.72). It also increased psychological need satisfaction (0.53, 95% CI [0.41, 0.65]) and PE engagement (0.46, 95% CI [0.37, 0.55]), while reducing psychological need frustration (−0.46, 95% CI [−0.57, −0.35]) and amotivation (−0.38, 95% CI [−0.47, −0.29]); effects on controlled motivation were small. title: The physiological demands of intermittent endurance exercise performed at different intensities within the anaerobic power reserve: Implications for fatigue development and performance
abstract: This study aimed to describe the physiological demands of intermittent endurance exercise (cycling) performed at different intensities within the anaerobic power reserve (APR); assess if these intensities are sustainable; and determine their effect on subsequent performance. On three separate days, endurance-trained males (n = 15, 36.2 ± 9.4 years old; 84.9 ± 13.0 kg) completed a high-intensity intermittent protocol consisting of fifteen 10-second high-intensity efforts (i.e., surges in intensity) separated by 50 seconds of low intensity (60% maximal aerobic power – MAP) work. These surges were performed either at the intensity associated with the participant’s MAP, or at 25% or 50% of their APR. A 30-second Wingate test (WG) was performed immediately after the protocol. Greater physiological and perceptual demands occurred during the APR conditions compared to MAP (p < .05), with very high demands occurring early in the protocol (surges 3–6) during the APR conditions. As such, only 8 and 4 participants completed all surges in the 25APR and 50APR conditions, respectively. Mean power output in the WG was significantly different between all conditions (p < .001), while maximal peak power (MPP) was only different between MAP and 50APR (p = .006). The results indicate that intermittent work at 25% and 50% APR lead to rapid increases in key physiological markers, altering the intramuscular environment, resulting in both severe leg discomfort and a perceived inability to cope with recurring surges. Consequently, the ability to perform a finishing sprint is also affected. title: Video-Based Coaching in Essentials in Minimally Invasive Gynecologic Surgery (EMIGS): A Randomized Controlled Trial.
abstract: To determine the effect of video-based coaching on skill acquisition for Essentials in Minimally Invasive Gynecologic Surgery (EMIGS). Single-site randomized controlled trial. Academic institution. Obstetrics and Gynecology residents (PGY1-PGY4) and medical students (MS3-MS4). Participants were randomized to a control cohort without video-based coaching or an intervention cohort with video-based coaching, where participants' surgical video was critiqued and the participant was given individualized strategies to improve performance. All participants underwent a baseline evaluation performing EMIGS tasks, followed by repeat testing after one month. After randomization, there were no significant demographic differences between cohorts with respect to level of training, prior laparoscopic experience, or days between completion of initial and final tasks. Baseline laparoscopic performance did not differ between cohorts. After the intervention, participants in the coaching cohort improved their time to complete the running suture task (Task 5) by a median of 250 seconds, compared with a 60-second improvement in the control cohort (p = 0.011). Medical students experienced a large effect, with a 361-second improvement in Task 5 performance compared with 80 seconds in controls (p = 0.032). Residents with coaching improved by 196 seconds compared with 60 seconds in resident controls (p = 0.083). Video-based coaching improved EMIGS Task 5 acquisition. EMIGS curricula within residency programs may benefit from incorporating video-based coaching to improve task acquisition.

title: An integrated quantitative framework for multidimensional player assessment in youth football.
Comparative effects of internal and external feedback during learning of a complex motor skill.
venue: The Journal of sports medicine and physical fitness
abstract: The influence of attentional focus on motor learning has been widely studied, yet evidence regarding how focus effects vary across learning stages and complex tasks remains inconclusive. The present study examined the impact of external vs. internal focus instructions on the acquisition and short-term retention of a complex manual skill task. Sixteen healthy novice adults (8 males and 8 females; mean age: 26.3±3.8 years), with no prior experience in twirling or organized sports participation, were randomly assigned to either an external focus (EFA) or an internal focus (IFA) instructional group. Following an initial familiarization phase, participants completed three acquisition blocks of 15 trials each (45 practice trials in total) and a 15-trial retention test performed the following day. Performance was evaluated in terms of movement effectiveness and technical execution quality. Participants receiving EFA instructions exhibited superior performance improvements during acquisition and higher retention scores than those receiving IFA instructions. Between-group comparisons revealed significant differences favoring the EFA group across all execution categories (all P<.05). These findings contribute to the understanding of how attentional focus manipulations influence motor behavior across learning stages, highlighting the potential utility of external focus strategies in complex motor tasks. Limitations related to sample size and instructional content are discussed, and implications for future research on attentional mechanisms in motor learning are considered.

title: Clustering professional football players using Gaussian mixture models: A case study of the English Premier League 2024/25
abstract: The increasing availability of detailed football performance data has created new opportunities for identifying player archetypes and informing recruitment and tactical decision-making. Most existing clustering approaches assign each player to a single group, despite the reality that many modern footballers perform hybrid roles spanning multiple stylistic categories. Performance data for 314 outfield players from the 2024/25 English Premier League season are analysed using a Gaussian mixture model (GMM) applied to principal component representations of player statistics. Unlike hard-assignment methods such as k-means, the GMM provides probabilistic cluster memberships, allowing uncertainty and role hybridity to be quantified. Seven player archetypes are identified in the full dataset. Posterior membership probabilities reveal a subset of players whose profiles span multiple clusters, providing an objective measure of tactical flexibility and stylistic ambiguity. Further analyses within defender, midfielder, and forward groups recover position-specific sub-archetypes and highlight exceptional outliers. The results demonstrate that model-based clustering provides a flexible and interpretable framework for identifying latent structure in high-dimensional performance data while explicitly quantifying uncertainty in cluster membership. More broadly, the approach is readily transferable to other sports and domains in which individuals exhibit overlapping characteristics and cannot be adequately represented by hard cluster assignments alone.
